utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Two procedural issues. First, we received a new set of potential exhibits by Mr. Krajisnik. We'll follow the same procedure as we did previously. That is, copies will be given to the parties to consider, perhaps assisted by language assistants or by native speakers to see whether this material is of a kind that could assist their case. Then, of course, we have to consider whether or not it should be translated. The Chamber, of course, always leaves it open that it could ask for any of these materials to be tendered into evidence at the request of the Chamber but the Chamber would first like to wait for the parties to see whether they think it could be -- could assist them in the presentation of their case. Of course, the Prosecution has presented its case already, but since it's now provided by Mr. Krajisnik, it might be new material for the Prosecution. So therefore it will be distributed. Second issue, the Prosecution, until now, had to guess on which of the 15 days would be for the Prosecution and which would be for the Chamber, since we said 15 days cross-examination and questions by the Bench. One of the reasons why the Chamber left that open until now is that, of course, we did not know to what extent the Prosecution would put questions to the witness which the Chamber had in mind as well. I mean, it's difficult to say exactly prior even to the beginning of the cross-examination whether most of the issues would be covered by the Prosecution. Taking into account the way matters went until now, and also encouraging the Prosecution to even improve the efficiency of the examination of Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber at this moment - but we have started only since a couple of days - has in mind that most likely we would end up with a division like 11 days Prosecution, four days Chamber. This is not final, but I can imagine that the Prosecution would like to have some guidance as to what to expect. And again, this is not a final decision. It also depends on what will happen in the days to come. The Prosecution has taken until now a little bit over four days. This week gives another four days. So therefore it would be next week, Wednesday approximately, that the Prosecution should head for finishing its cross-examination. If our assessment on the division of time would meanwhile change, we'll inform the parties. Then Mr. Tieger. You may proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I raise two matters, please, Your Honour? Firstly, so far as the first matter that Your Honour has raised this morning is concerned, is there an accompanying CD?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an accompanying CD, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That could we be provided as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is only one, first of all I have to take care that it's copied. That goes relatively easy. There is -- the second document is a -- is a -- just a listing of files on that CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Secondly, we went to see Mr. Krajisnik this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first thing he did -- I beg your pardon, this afternoon, shortly before the Chamber sat. First thing did he was to try and draw to my attention various comments that he's got about the destruction material that has been served by the Prosecution on the Defence. Could I ask to see him again at one of the two breaks today to discuss that with him? I deliberately said I needed to ask the Chamber's permission, although looking back on the record, I note Your Honour has suggested I do that in any event at an earlier stage in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is no problem. Perhaps I did not fully understand it. You said comments he received or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That he's made. He's been given the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got a copy of the material, and he wants to draw various comments to my attention because, Your Honour, our deadline to respond, at the moment, is the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No problem. You may further discuss any comments Mr. Krajisnik has on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on the material received. I didn't ask whether the Prosecution would have any objections against it. I should have asked, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just a couple of matters fairly quickly, I think, before we move to a different subject. First of all, it's correct, isn't it, that on April -- turning your attention back to the beginning of April, 1992, as we were discussing last week. And it's correct, isn't it, that on April 3rd, 1992, you telephoned Mr. Zepinic and asked him to come to a meeting at the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met with Mr. Zepinic at my office. There were representatives of the MUP who had called him; I didn't call him. But I did meet with him. I don't know whether it was the 3rd but it was on the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that meeting, Mr. Zepinic tendered and you accepted his resignation as the deputy minister of the joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know, and I was not the one who had to accept his resignation. He had to submit it to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina because he was their staff. I must have known then that he had resigned in anger because he had a quarrel with MUP representatives. I neither demanded nor accepted his resignation. I had no authority to demand it. Maybe I just discussed it with him. Because he was appointed by the government not by the president of the Serbian Assembly, and he wasn't our staff member. Before that, the Ministerial Council was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me -- and perhaps -- first of all, perhaps I misspoke with regard to the date. It may have been April 4th, but I take it that you weren't fixed on the particular date of April 3rd rather than April 4th in answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of those dates. You're right. I can't remember exactly which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And secondly, the meeting to which I'm referring would be a meeting at which you and Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic, among others, would have been present.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I was there, Mandic, Stanisic and Zepinic were there. I don't know about Karadzic or others. I know it was at my office at the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the subject matter of that particular meeting was the splitting of the Special Forces of the joint MUP, the splitting of the unit on an ethnic basis, and Mr. Zepinic's role or failure to act in connection with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All is correct apart from the last bit. Issues of the MUP were the subject of discussion, especially the special units of the MUP. As for failure to act, it wasn't exactly like that, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- at the time of the meeting, it's correct, isn't it, that your understanding and the others' -- understanding of the others present whom you mentioned, was that Mr. Zepinic was either blocking or not facilitating the split of the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to tell you exactly what happened to avoid any confusion? I know exactly what happened. It's not true that he was blocking the split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention -- and I don't know if you have the tabs in front of you -- to tab 97. And before I ask you any questions about that, Mr. Krajisnik, let me ask you one additional question. I had asked you earlier about Mr. Zepinic's resignation. Did you seek or accept on that occasion Mr. Zepinic's resignation as -- resignation from the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that you've ever asked me about Zepinic. This is the first time you're asking me. If you did ask me before, would you please remind me. I don't think I discussed Zepinic and his resignation before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't turning your attention back to questions before today. Just noting that I had asked you a question about his resignation and I think your answer focussed on his resignation from the Bosnian MUP, and I simply wanted to clarify whether you sought or obtained Mr. Zepinic's resignation from either the Bosnian MUP or the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sitting there while they argued. They argued all the time. And I didn't have a word with Mr. Zepinic and I didn't ask for his resignation. All that he did and all that he wrote, I know it's not true. I was just there while they were attacking him. They attacked him even before, over that special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Zepinic ultimately submit his resignation; and if so, to whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to believe me when I say that I don't know. I just saw the resignation. Whether he submitted it to somebody then and there, I don't know. He didn't submit it to me. He was to submit it to the government. The Ministerial Council had already been dissolved. He had no post, no position, in the Assembly or the Serbian Assembly. The only authority he could submit it to was the government, because the government appoints ministers, not the Assembly. I couldn't do anything about it. I don't remember to whom he submitted his resignation. I don't know whether I was asked about this before. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated I wanted to turn your attention to tab 97, and if we can look at that quickly now, that's a record of a statement given by Mr. Zepinic to the state security officials of the Republika Srpska MUP a few days before his arrest as, I believe, an enemy of the state, but we can look at the specific allegations. On -- at the top of page 3 of the English, and also at the top of page 3 of the B/C/S, Mr. Zepinic stated that, "Momcilo Krajisnik, the chairman of the BiH Assembly, called me during the meeting --" he relates on the previous page "-- on the phone and asked me to go to his cabinet after the meeting. After the meeting, I went to see Krajisnik and Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic --" and others, including the people you mentioned; Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic, and we see Mr. Karadzic, all of whom were already there. He indicates further that, upon arriving, he was immediately attacked by those present because of the meeting he had held with the special unit, since the division of the special unit had been agreed upon before. Now, Mr. Zepinic indicates, the division would be impossible, referring to the meeting he had with other members of the special unit and to the fact that his actions had seemingly prevented that. "Now the division would be impossible," he stated, "since Repija and Maric would not participate in it because these two were bigger authorities in the special units than Vikic or Karisik." Now, is that essentially the situation, Mr. Krajisnik, that the subject of the meeting was the fact that those present had learned that Mr. Zepinic had met with certain members of the special unit and that his contact with them was making the division of the special unit impossible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is this: They had agreed about the division of the unit in the presence of Mr. Zepinic. I had nothing to do with it and I didn't know about it. In the meantime, Mr. Zepinic met with Mr. Delimustafic or I don't know who else, and then he changed his mind and interpreted this agreement differently. And those people from the MUP complained about him. It wasn't I who called up Mr. Zepinic. It's probably the secretary who invited him, and he came. Many things stated here are correct. They did attack him. But I was not one of those who attacked him. I sat there all the time and observed, and he was really under fierce attack for going back on his decision and for practically going back on that agreement. That's how I understood it. As for resignations, I never got an offer of a resignation from him, nor did I demand it. And anyway, I would have been the wrong person to submit a resignation to because he had nothing to do with me. He knew exactly who had appointed him. He could have offered his resignation elsewhere. I did not attack him. My close family took him out of Sarajevo in the back of the car, in the boot of the car. They saved him. He lives in Australia. You can call him up and ask him. I don't know to whom he gave this statement. I thought he had given a statement to the Serb MUP, but I see from this document that it was the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, you're correct, Mr. Krajisnik. It was to the Serb MUP, and that's clear from the context of the document itself and also from Mr. Zepinic's arrest a few days later by the Serb MUP. Could I ask you to turn quickly to tab 98, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 98, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. That's a document dated April 4th, 1992, from Mr. Zepinic to the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the attention of Mr. President and the subject is a resignation letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Tieger, could I just ask one question in relation to one of the previous answers? Mr. Krajisnik, you told us that Mr. Zepinic did come and that you were not actively involved in this meeting where he arrived. You said, "I sat there all the time and observed, and he was really under fierce attack for going back on his decision and for practically going back on that agreement." In the statement, the meeting is described as you, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, Mr. Djeric, Mr. Simovic, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Karisik being present. What kind of a forum was that? I mean, what made these people to meet together? I mean, what -- why those persons? I mean, as far as I understand, it's not the Presidency, it's not what some people called the expanded Presidency, it's not the cabinet. It's -- what made this meeting be composed as it is described by Mr. Zepinic, if the description is correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the entire Presidency was there but I can answer your question. I was constantly at my office. People worked little and they dropped by. It was a very hard time. There was no special reason apart from the fact that those people from the MUP had raised the issue then. It was a completely informal meeting. It was not called in advance and it was nothing special. Very often Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Karadzic, and Buha and MPs would drop by to see me. It was nothing special. It was not a group. All of them were some sort of officials, either in Bosnia and Herzegovina or in our Assembly. They would drop by like to have coffee. Not exactly like that, but it was nothing special either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was at what time of the day, Mr. Krajisnik, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. I worked from dusk until dawn. I can't really remember. It wasn't by night. That's not what I mean. I think it was in daytime but I wouldn't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because Mr. Zepinic describes it as "When I arrived home in the evening," that some people called him and asked whether he could drop by since they had heard everything on television. "I accepted their suggestion immediately," only they had a meeting the next day. Yes. Now, thank you for your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. I think Mr. Tieger was taking you to tab 98.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I heard was 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, His Honour is correct; 98, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be the resignation to which -- resignation letter and the resignation to which Mr. Zepinic refers in his statement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I mean probably. It probably is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was reference made to Mr. Mandic's authorisation during your testimony on Friday. We've already had an opportunity to review the -- both the conclusions of the Ministerial Council at its meeting on January 11 and the formation of the steering committee of Serbian cadres of the MUP formed pursuant to those conclusions. That's the meeting on February 11th that was discussed earlier. And at that meeting on February 11th, Mr. Mandic was placed in charge of the Serbian advisory board which was responsible for carrying out all preparations for the functioning of the Serbian MUP. I'd like also to bring your attention to another document found, I believe, at tab 101 -- I think 101. And that would be a decision of 6 February, 1992 -- not a decision but a -- well, an order or authorisation by Dr. Karadzic as president of the SDS referring to personnel matters regarding the MUP, and if you could turn, please, to the third section of that order by Dr. Karadzic, found on the second page, and it's headed III, it states: "I hereby authorise and order Mr. Momcilo Mandic, assistant in the MUP of BH, to participate in solving personnel and organisational matters in the MUP of BH on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party." So would it be correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that by February of 1992, Mr. Zepinic [sic] had the authorisation from Dr. Karadzic for responsibility to solve personnel and organisational matters in the MUP in addition to the responsibilities which he received from the steering committee of Serbian cadres for carrying out all preparations for the functioning of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was not interpreted very well. I don't know what this steering committee is. Can I look at the original to see what the Serbian for "steering committee" is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's located at tab 100, Mr. Krajisnik, if it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While you're taking that moment, perhaps I can correct the transcript. It states at 12 -- page -- excuse me, page 12, line 5, that -- I can only assume it took it down correctly and I asked the question incorrectly: "Would it be correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that by February, 1992, Mr. Zepinic had the authorisation from Dr. Karadzic?" and, of course, we were talking about Mr. Mandic's authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not an authorisation. This is what it's all about: The person in the SDS who was in charge of appointing personnel was Mr. Karadzic, with Mr. Dukic. However, implementation of agreements was always the job of ranking representatives of the region concerned. Since -- or rather, the jurisdiction concerned. Since Mr. Zepinic was the highest-ranking Serb staff member in the police, his job was to implement the agreed appointments. And now, Mr. Mandic, similarly, got the authorisation to implement what had been agreed, not to decide on appointments himself. Because Mr. Zepinic no longer enjoyed the confidence of the Serbian Democratic Party, and that's what Mr. Mandic himself said here when he testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with that clarification, then, that would reflect in so far as -- that would reflect two of the authorities that Mr. Mandic enjoyed as of February 1992, then. That is the one referred to in tab 101 bestowed by Dr. Karadzic, and that indicated in the document at tab 100, the -- reflected in the minutes of the meeting on February 11, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic had no other authority, no other powers. This record that you've just mentioned, I saw it here for the first time, and Mr. Mandic himself had explained that they had met in Banja Luka on their own initiative to discuss problems of the MUP. It was their internal meeting. And Mr. Mandic did not have any powers, if you mean the dispatch, because at that time there was a minister and there was a Prime Minister of the Serb Republic who had to be consulted, should he have sent it on behalf of some sort of Serb MUP. He had absolutely no powers. As for staffing issues, Mr. Mandic only had the obligation to implement what the parties had agreed amongst themselves, because Mr. Zepinic did not do it. In other words, to implement the appointments that people from the SDA were blocking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point -- if I could distribute one more document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had indicated in response to your comment about the statement that I would provide the decision regarding Mr. Zepinic's arrest or being taken into custody, and that's the document before you. And as you can see, it's dated September 2nd, 1992, bearing the names at the bottom, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I don't have any particular questions about that. It had come up during the course of the question and answer and I wanted it to be presented to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want, I can give you a comment. It would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I presented it to you only in connection with the issue of whether or not the statement -- to whom the statement was given or to which agency the statement was given. Insofar as I'm concerned, that are the only questions I have about the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you said that he tendered his resignation in me in April and this was part of the protocol of the Serb Assembly. He didn't give it to me. You saw it written down; the 4th of April. For four months he was in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so he did not resign. He was there. He held that post. And only when he got fed up down there, when they wanted to kill him, then he came to Serb territory. That's the whole truth. And then they arrested him here and then they let him go, although there was -- there were criminal charges brought against him, but then he was in this car boot and he got to Serbia and ultimately to Australia, so that was the point and that's the way it actually happened. For five months during the war in 1992, he was there with them after this resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am also advised that tab 101 needs a number, and I'm sorry, I led the Registry to put those out of order. But I don't think it will cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, tab 101 seems to be a -- yes -- a document issued by president of the BH SDS, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, dated the 6th of February, 1992. Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1207, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this point I'd like to yield, at least momentarily, to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- yes. Mr. Krajisnik, you said Mr. Zepinic did not tender his resignation in April and then you later on said because he stayed for another couple of months with them. The resignation seems to be addressed to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and "staying with them," I understand to be staying with Bosnia and Herzegovina, not necessarily the Serbian Republic. So I'm not quite sure that I fully understood what you meant to say there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, he tendered his resignation as deputy minister in the joint MUP. It was sent to the wrong address, the protocol of the Serb Assembly. It was not in my office. I don't know where it was. So he was supposed to submit this resignation to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, after April, up until the month of September, he stayed on in Sarajevo. When I say "with them," I mean, well, I mean in Sarajevo. In the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This Muslim Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had he resigned then, in April, he would not have stayed there and he would not have been in the MUP. That's what I was trying to say. I mean, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the letter as such says that he is resigning, he addresses it, and you say he did wrongly so but he addresses it to the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he makes reference to the agreement on personnel policy realisation at the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that he is submitting irrevocable resignation. So the letter very much says that he resigns from a position in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or as you say that's wrong, he should have addressed the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's unclear to me, because what he did, at least from what appears from this letter, is different from what you considered that he should have done. Is that correct? A correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, he was appointed by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's only those who appoint him that can have him resign. You also have stenographic notes and transcripts of the Serb Assembly. Zepinic is not on the agenda at all. The president of the Assembly cannot remove him from that position. I didn't know about it. This was never at Assembly sessions. There were several Assemblies after that. And he didn't submit this resignation to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mean, he had -- he had no position, no post, in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Ministerial Council had been dissolved before he resigned, as a matter of fact. So this was just formal. This resignation doesn't make any sense at all. I mean, why would he submit it to me or the Assembly? We never appointed him; how can we remove him? Well, formally, he could have submitted it, say, to the party, but I guess it never crossed his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he is resigned from a position he never had. Did you ever receive this letter or did you never receive this letter? Apart from whether it was wrongly addressed to you, but did you ever receive it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I would be dishonest if I would say anything else. I don't know. I never paid any attention to this. I don't know. I guess then I would have put it on the agenda, had I known about his resignation. But he didn't carry this through because he stayed on in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger -- or, rather, Mr. Harmon, from what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one last question, Your Honour, about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Setting aside the question of technical or legal niceties with respect to the resignation, there is no question, is there, that this document, that is the resignation letter of April 4th, 1992, emerged from the meeting that we discussed a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether he wrote it. There were quarrels there and it's possible that he submitted this because everybody attacked him. I don't know. The war started the very next day. I had nothing to do with this. I have no idea who he gave it to, whatever. I have no idea. I know that everybody attacked him. I didn't. I was the host, so to speak, and frankly, since there were so many people there, I didn't have the time to say a word to him. I didn't agree with him anyway because he was unfair. I mean, why did he lie? Why didn't he say straight away, I don't agree with this? The background is different, but that's the point. I did not attack him. Quite simply, I was the host there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And yes, you're right, Mr. Harmon will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, forgive me if it has been said before. This letter by Dr. Zepinic addressed to the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 4th of April, where was that found?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll find out for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps one final question, I'm sorry, Mr. Harmon. That -- the stamp, Mr. Tieger, of what we find under tab 98 is translated as Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then illegible. First of all, I can already decipher "Sarajevo" so not everything is illegible what appears under that. Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I mumbled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're mumbling. I always take it these are meaningful mumbles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it says "Sarajevo" in the translation, bottom left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the stamp on the top right-hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. I was right to mumble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was focussing on the stamp. I mentioned the stamp, as a matter of fact. Of course, one of the things that's wondering me whether in one way or the other if it could be -- of course, it would be interesting to know whether the stamp, which might be a stamp of reception, would be from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or just of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so since "Sarajevo" is certainly legible, I would like, if you make any inquiries as to where there was found, I would like you to make some further inquiries as well as to whether we could decipher the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I make one, I hope, constructive suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I invite Your Honour to ask Mr. Krajisnik to read that stamp out as best he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if he's able to do so. Mr. Krajisnik, at the suggestion of Mr. Josse, I ask to you read in text in tab 98 whether you, perhaps by reconstructing the text, whether you, with a certain level of certitude, could decipher what it says in the stamp, at the right-hand top of that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can decipher, seems to point to this being the stamp of the Assembly of the Serbian people. However, I cannot read line 1 because it says down here in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it says Assembly. It could have been of the Serb people in this second line, but I cannot read the first line. I think that this is something like the offices. It's not Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's more probable that it will be the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All of this is written in Cyrillic. If it were Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would be both in Cyrillic and in the Roman script. This is the first time I see this stamp, by the way. I don't remember it from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the first line you're reading, your understanding that it says the Republican Assembly or Republican Skupstina, or is that what you take it from that first line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the second line. Looks like "Skupstina Srpska Narodna," "Assembly of the Serb People." And the third line "in Bosnia and Herzegovina" "U [phoen] Bosnia Herzegovina," and then "Sarajevo." But I don't know what line 1 is, so there is a bit of a reservation here because you can't see it properly, but it's not Bosnia-Herzegovina. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And by the E [phoen] in the beginning of the third line, you consider it to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could proceed by distributing, first of all, the next bundle of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, to keep ourselves organised, any reference being made to the lower numbers in the near future? Because otherwise the pile grows and grows. If not then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, there will not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a number of questions particularly and beginning with a response that you gave to one of Mr. Stewart's questions. You were asked by Mr. Stewart who was running the war in the period before the Assembly session that occurred on the 12th of May, 1992, and your answer was that it was the armed people, and you went on further to assert that up to that point in time, the JNA was neutral to a maximum - and I'm quoting your answer. You also asserted that the policy of the Yugoslav People's Army was to be equidistant to all sides and have the role of an intermediary. Those are the assertions that I would like to explore with you, Mr. Krajisnik. To begin with, there is no dispute that both JNA and the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs shared similar views on preserving the integrity of the state of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indeed, they worked closely together, the leadership of both what became the Republika Srpska and the JNA to achieve that end.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not fully confirm that answer that you provided. We were in contact but we did not work together. You see the report of the 2nd Military District where they treat us equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, first of all, to an intercept. It will need a new number. It is found in tab 110. Mr. Krajisnik, if you could direct your attention to tab 110, and if I could get a number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1208, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I ask you, both on the 15th and on the 16th of May, the neutrality to a maximum was mentioned by Mr. Krajisnik. Could you tell me which one you had in mind so that I can have a look at it. The first one is he's talking about the army was neutral, the other one it was I think that the JNA was neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 15th, that reference is found at 94109. Starting -- the answer starting at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Day 15, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Day 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Day 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a different numbering. Day 15 of his testimony or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the reference I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check. I'll find out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I can get that, Your Honour, in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is an intercept I'd like you to cast your eye on. This is a conversation that occurred between Radovan Karadzic and General Simovic, General Tomislav Simovic. It was held on the 2nd of November, 1991. I'd like you to cast your eye on that for just a moment. While you're examining that intercept, Mr. Krajisnik, do you know who General Tomislav Simovic was and do you know which position he held in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a general. I mean, I heard of General Simovic. He held a high position in Belgrade. I could not define it exactly, unless he was, say, in security or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I were to inform you that he was the Serbian minister of defence, would you accept that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. Well, possibly. I don't know. I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reference to Mr. Krajisnik's testimony is on the 16th of May, for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in this conversation between Dr. Karadzic and General Simovic, if you turn to page -- the page in the B/C/S bearing in the upper right-hand corner the ERN 03236325, it is the second page in the B/C/S. And Your Honours, if Your Honours also turn to the second page. I want to refer Your Honours and Mr. Krajisnik to the following dialogue between Dr. Karadzic and General Simovic: "Radovan Karadzic: How are you? "General Simovic: It could be better, but as long as Bosnia is ours it is fine. "Radovan Karadzic: Well, how long will Bosnia be ours? "General Simovic: As long as you are there, and I am here." Now, this intercept goes on at the bottom of the page, Mr. Krajisnik, to discuss the purpose, why Dr. Karadzic is calling General Simovic. He says, at the bottom of page 2 in the English, and it's just below the part I read to you in B/C/S, he is describing a big problem with Uzelac, who, according to Dr. Karadzic, "he lacks five to 6.000 people. He's short of equipment." and something urgently has to be done to assist him. Dr. Karadzic, I'm referring to page 3, in the middle of page 3, and, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm referring to the third page in the B/C/S, the third box. Dr. Karadzic says that he was working on arranging to have "two and a half thousand guys from Ozren to go there to him, but I'm afraid he does not even have equipment there." If you turn, finally, Mr. Krajisnik, to the fourth page in the B/C/S, and, Your Honours, to the fourth page in the English, third box from the bottom, Dr. Karadzic, in his conversation with General Simovic, says: "I gave the order, I gave the order to all the municipalities there and all the presidents of the municipalities. I gave the order, they introduced the command posts. They also introduced --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said page 3, but I can't find it -- oh, sorry, here it is. It's page 3. The third box, rather, in Serbian. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me carry on with what I was reading I'll start again, actually: "I gave the order --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "I gave the order, I gave the order to all the municipalities there and all the presidents of the municipalities. I gave the order, they introduced the command posts. They also introduced the wartime, completely wartime, wartime conditions of economy and work and all. I announced general mobilisation to them because it is going -- it is ongoing, from earlier on, like, er, so I said they had to hand over the military conscripts, and so on." And then he goes on in that same box to say: "I'm asking you to see a bit with Slobo and with Adzic and Kadijevic if they want us to save a part of the country this is the chance when." If you go down further, two boxes down, Dr. Karadzic says: "Well, that is the problem. We have to do something here. I gave the order to provide 10.000 people there in one week, I gave the order and now that order is given again, it is being issued this very moment." Finally, Mr. Krajisnik, if I can turn you to the last page in the B/C/S, and if I can turn the Court, refer the Court to page 5 of the English translation, third box from the bottom, part way into that particular box, Dr. Karadzic says: "The most important thing for us is that here, on their map, on their threshold, that we stop them, that we fortify the Western Slavonian front and put all the Serbian villages under control -- and we put all the Serbian villages under control. That is the most important thing on the point -- and the point on which Yugoslavia survives." Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know my learned friend hasn't asked his question yet, but I am hesitant for him to ask any question until Mr. Krajisnik has had an opportunity to briefly cast his eye over the rest of this. It's very different to when I was asking questions about intercepts, because I knew that Mr. Krajisnik had read all of those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you please read to such an extent that you have a fair impression of what this telephone conversation tells you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Thank you. Thank you for -- thank you to Mr. Josse for protecting me. That's very useful. Please go ahead, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to examine that intercept, Mr. Krajisnik? Okay. Now this intercept --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't read the whole intercept but I want to be as expeditious as possible so that I don't use up too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I want you to be as accurate as possible as well, so if you need the time, take it, Mr. Krajisnik. This intercept clearly shows that the minister of defence, General Simovic, and Dr. Karadzic are working jointly together in an effort to preserve the former Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'll tell you, because I don't know anything about this conversation but I'll tell you what Mr. Karadzic was advocating. Western Slavonia was -- there was a counter-propaganda going on and two-thirds of Western Slavonia, of Serb villages, had withdrawn, creating a real exodus, moving into Republika Srpska. What happened was really horrific, and here, Mr. Karadzic, is calling and asking for the protection of this area because, he says, it's treason. There was a party from Serbia that was blamed for it because they had withdrawn their men, there were not enough men, and they had to ask for volunteers. Everybody had pulled out - I don't know how many people were driven out by the Croats - and if this is Mr. Simovic, the minister of defence, as you say - I take your word for it - the request is that he help General Uzelac, who was commander of the corps in Banja Luka, and he had those villages on the territory of Croatia under his jurisdiction. That's what I know. As for cooperation, there are several telephone conversations in which Mr. Uzelac called up Mr. Karadzic, because he realised there was only one political party supporting him there, asking Mr. Karadzic to promote mobilisation, to promote the call-up, to help the defence of that area. That's how I understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us turn to another document. If you could turn to tab 125. And Mr. Krajisnik, if I can -- this is the plebiscite speech. This is already an exhibit in the case. It's Prosecution Exhibit 1191. Mr. Krajisnik, if I can direct your attention to the second-to-last page in the B/C/S, it bears an ERN number 00270638 at the bottom, and if I can direct Your Honour's attention to page 10, to the last paragraph, again, focusing on the unity of view between the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs, Dr. Karadzic says, and I quote: "So that's it. There will probably be more discussions and questions concerning the army. Please, Serbs do not need any party army. There is an army here. By chance, their aims and our aims coincide 100 per cent." Now, that speech, Mr. Krajisnik, was a speech that was given in November of 1991, and you can see in that speech that Dr. Karadzic has the view that the aims of the JNA and the -- his own views, the views of the Bosnian Serbs, coincide 100 per cent. And that's the case, isn't it, at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not. I have to tell you that Karadzic thought they did, and I thought they did, but it wasn't true, because the army, soon afterwards, left our region, pulled out, and took the weapons with them. However, at this point, Karadzic expressed what he was thinking, what we were all thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wanting to preserve Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So at that point in time, Dr. Karadzic, at least, believed that the views of the army and the views of the JNA were essentially in -- 100 per cent together in their views? That's what Dr. Karadzic expressed at this point in time. I want to direct your attention, sir, to the tab, document found in tab 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1209, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is really two documents, Mr. Krajisnik. What I want to do is I want to direct your attention first of all to the document that is found on the second page of the B/C/S, the document that is dated the 10th of December, 1991. It is from the federal Secretariat for National Defence, SFRY armed forces Main Staff, it is a military secret, strictly confidential, and it is entitled, "Directive on the use of the armed forces for the preparation and performance of combat operations in the forthcoming period." And the author of this document is the federal secretary for national defence, General Kadijevic. Now, this -- first of all, have you seen this document before, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the first page, I, the three paragraphs in there, and the first paragraph under II. Now, in this directive, Mr. Krajisnik, the first three paragraphs under I, General Kadijevic is talking about the Yugoslav crisis, and essentially in paragraphs 2 and 3, is looking back at the developments in Croatia, and he's discussing the events at -- following the fall of Vukovar and events in the political developments. But if we go to paragraph 2, General Kadijevic - II - General Kadijevic looks ahead, in other words, he's looking ahead to the future beyond the 10th of December of 1991. Let me read this part into the record: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for the accomplishments -- for accomplishing the ultimate goals of the war: Protection of the Serbian population, a peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, and the creation of conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you went to Belgrade on a number of occasions, your colleagues went to Belgrade on a number of occasions, Dr. Karadzic, other representatives of the Bosnian Serbs, and in the discussions that you had and your colleagues had with both military and political leaders, the protection of the Serbian people was a central topic of discussion; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main thing is that our cooperation with the JNA took place in Sarajevo, with General Kukanjac, and when I spoke about cooperation I spoke about people who were in Sarajevo. Now as for people who were in Belgrade, I did not have many meetings with them. But it is true that there was one meeting of that kind, maybe two. All they wanted to do was to perform their constitutional role, to preserve peace. Why is it written Serb people here? Because the Slovenes turned against the JNA. Croats too. Muslims had already voted for sovereignty by that time and started creating problems in Bosnia. They had nobody else who wanted to preserve Yugoslavia apart from Serbs in Croatia and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were minorities. Right here, Mr. Kadijevic - and I don't need to emphasise this - he is not a Serb, he's half Serb, half Croat, he was dedicated, he was really committed to Yugoslavia. He wasn't saying this because he was a Serb but because Serbs needed protection. He was a committed Yugoslav. That's how I understood him. And in all the contacts I've seen him in, he was always in favour of preserving peace and protecting those who needed protection, those who were vulnerable. But on his territory, Serbs were the only ones who were responding to mobilisation, to call-ups, and the others had turned against the JNA and became enemies, and Serbs were in the minority, all the way until the end of 1991, and I'm speaking now about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, my question was this, and I want to know if you're disputing this: In the meetings that representatives of your government had with Slobodan Milosevic, with representatives of -- from the federal government, the issue of the protection of the Serbian people was an issue that was discussed. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the Serbian people. I'm speaking sincerely. Slobodan Milosevic is dead. He spoke more about the protection of Muslims than the protection of Serbs. He's no longer with us. He's no longer on trial. But I'm telling you the way it was. He -- I'm telling you what is true and what is correct. Kadijevic and Milosevic are no longer alive and, of course, we were interested in the fate of Serbs. I have responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would first answer the question. The question was not whether the protection of the Serbian people was more important than the protection of any other people. The question simply was whether the issue of the protection of the Serbian people was an issue that was discussed. Is that correct or not? Because you did not, and if so only indirectly, answer the question. Was it an issue? Perhaps not the most important one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was a topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, looking at the clock, are we going to take a break at 4.00 or are we going to go past 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to take a break. We had a late start, which means that we have to break also a quarter of an hour later. If this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were still dealing with the document that is found in tab 109, and if you could turn to the first page of that tab, I had finished exploring with you the directive of General Kadijevic. The document on the first page is also dated the 10th of December, 1991. It's a transmission letter that accompanied the directive. It is, as I say, dated the 10th of December, 1991. It is a military secret, strictly confidential. The copy that was transmitted on this occasion to the 9th Corps was a copy number 25, and the text of this transmission letter reads: "We hereby enclose the Directive of the Federal Secretary for National Defence on the use of the armed forces in the forthcoming period." So it is clear, Mr. Krajisnik, that as of the 10th of December, what was transmitted from the federal Secretariat of National Defence to subordinate units of the JNA - in this case to the 9th Corps commander - was the directive of General Kadijevic in which he outlined the ultimate aims of the war, which included the protection of the Serbian population. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you testified that while there had been discussions about the protection of the Serbian people, that those discussions had taken place prior to the commencement of the war, specifically, Mr. Krajisnik, did you personally become aware, through any source, through -- at any period of time up to the 12th of May, 1992, that the JNA's actions and conduct was directed toward the protection of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I learned about it, but it was implied. I understood that, that the JNA was supposed to and was our guarantor. That was my firm conviction. Because let me just remind you that in all our papers we said we were not going to attack anybody, we only want protection because we are a minority. You have that statement by Mr. Karadzic at the Assembly session on the 27th of March. We were relying to a great extent on the JNA as our protector. I believe I even sent a letter asking them to protect us at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That is an exhibit already in this trial. Mr. Krajisnik, on the 18th of March, 1992, at the 11th session of the Assembly, where you and others reported on the latest session of the conference on the Cutileiro developments, you are quoted in the Assembly session as saying, and I quote: "I think the problem is that they want BH to be -- Bosnia-Herzegovina to be internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. In this respect, it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons, if we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground, that we start determining the territory and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way." Now, after the Cutileiro sessions concluded on the 18th of March, 1992, there was another session in the negotiations in Lisbon on the 31st of March, 1992. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the end of March, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And thereafter, another session was to be called on the 1st of May, 1992, in Lisbon, and I believe you and Dr. Karadzic and others attended that session, but ultimately that session was called off because of a failure to honour a cease-fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went to Lisbon and then we went to Graz to meet with the Croats. Mr. Izetbegovic did not come but Mr. Silajdzic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this Trial Chamber has heard considerable evidence, as have you, Mr. Krajisnik, about events on the ground between the 18th of March, 1992, and the 12th of May, 1992, and I want to focus your attention on some of that evidence. Mr. Krajisnik, if you could turn first of all to tab 103. Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to be directing your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we have not received any index, so it's difficult for us --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, you don't have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least -- unless it's in one of the other indexes, but at least it's not on the top of this bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if I can remedy that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because then I don't have to ask you whether something is in evidence or not because it's usually indicated on the index.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is an exhibit number, I was going to say, on this particular exhibit, Your Honour. In any event, it's Prosecution Exhibit 184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- Your Honours, I'm going to be directing your attention to page 2, paragraph 4, about a third of the way down. And Mr. Krajisnik, if you go in, in the B/C/S version, it is pages 3 and 4, about a little below halfway down on that page, the page that bears ERN number 00478674. Now, this is a document that is the war record of the 6th Infantry Brigade, Colonel Branko Basara, and evidence that has been adduced in this trial is that Colonel Basara was a JNA officer, and I want to direct your attention to those portions beginning on page 3. Mr. Krajisnik, I will read --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 674 being the last number; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, 674. And about, probably -- on the B/C/S copy it looks about a little below halfway down the page, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Basara, according to this record, this war record, says, and I quote, "With the arrival of the brigade on this territory, the Muslims and the Croats became afraid and the Serbs heaved a sigh of relief." And I'll skip the next sentence and continue reading: "We ordered the Serbs to arm themselves quickly and replenished the units, since our task, as a JNA unit, was to prevent conflicts between the nationalities, that is to prevent the slaughter of the Serbian people, we could not publicly arm the Serbs. We then worked along two lines. The first was organising and arming the Serbian people. And the second was negotiating and persuading the Muslims and Croats to remain loyal and that we could live together. The negotiations dealt with the share out of power. We had to resort to a trick to make it possible for to us arm the Serbs publicly and legally. The story was devised that the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps had ordered the 6th to be promoted from a light to an infantry brigade and that it could have as many as 15 battalions, that the brigade should be demobilised as soon as possible. So that the Muslims and Croats would not enlist in the brigade, it was put about that as soon as mobilisation finished, it was leaving for Kupres. Then conditions were made to legally arm and form nine battalions. In addition to this, the battalion was armed in Kotor Varos and one in the Kljuc Brigade. We also helped considerably in arming the Ministry of the Interior in Banja Luka." 20 Now, if we go down to paragraph 5 of this letter, then we are going to -- Colonel Basara is going to be discussing what his unit did in Bosanska Krupa, and Bosanska Krupa, according to the 1991 census, was a Muslim majority municipality. Paragraph 5: "Take time from the battle report for the liberation of Krupa. The Muslims considered Bosanska Krupa to be a fortress and that the Serbs could not liberate it. Following a call from the Serbs in Krupa that about 200 fighters from the Territorial Defence surrounded in the area of the department store needed to be freed, volunteers were collected and they set out. About 150 fighters were engaged in the operation with the support of armoured combat vehicles, mortars, 128 millimetre guns and rockets. The operation was carried out swiftly and effectively. The enemy forces were scattered and heavy losses were inflicted on them. By nightfall on the same day we emerged on the Una River. Since we belonged to the JNA, we were not allowed to reveal our results." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from victims from Bosanska Krupa who have testified that on the 21st and the 22nd of April, 1992, the municipality was taken over by both the JNA and local Serbs. And at the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, you may recall that Mr. Vjestica stood up and he reported about the takeover of the municipality, and he said, among other things, Mr. Krajisnik, "What have we done in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa? I must tell you to remind you that there was only 24 per cent of Serbs in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. There is 14.500 of us and there is 47.000 Muslims. For a year and a half we have been preparing for the war in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa because we knew there -- that there would be war and that it could not be avoided." Went on to say, at the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik: "That was what we claimed and that is why we did get to the right bank of the Una River. On the right bank of the Una River there are no more Muslims in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa." Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Vjestica described very dramatic events that took place in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, that took place prior to the intended negotiations on the 1st of May that were to take place in Lisbon. Were you aware, Mr. Krajisnik, prior to going to Lisbon on the 1st of May, or prior to the 12th of May, 1992, that the Bosnian Serbs had taken power in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa and that they had done so with the assistance of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know and they did not take over power. They took over just half of Bosanska Krupa because the Una River separates the Krupa river -- the Una River in two parts [as interpreted]. On the right-hand side there is only Radusa, one single Muslim village. The other villages are Serb. And I didn't know that they had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- so when Mr. Vjestica raised that with you at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, that was a revelation to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vjestica explained it all to you in that interview. He told it to you here as a witness, as an accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was that, when Mr. Vjestica stood up at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, and revealed the dramatic events that he reported, was that a revelation to you? Was that the first time you had heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Maybe I've heard about it in some form or other, but I don't remember it. I understood his contribution as an exaggeration, a well-meant one - there was nothing ill-intentioned about it - and he explained it all in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's take a look at tab 104, which is already exhibited, Your Honours. It's Prosecution Exhibit 168. This deals with Sanski Most, which is another municipality that was a Muslim-majority municipality. And this is a municipality, the evidence that's been produced in this Court, is that the JNA and the Serbian Territorial Defence took over power in that municipality on the 19th of April, 1992. And if we turn to the exhibit that is in front of you, Mr. Krajisnik, this is a -- first of all, let me identify it. It's an order from the commander of the Sanski Most Territorial Defence, and you will see, at item number 4, it says as follows: "I have decided to defend, with Serbian --" I'm sorry: "I have decided: To defend sectors with Serbian settlements and vital facilities in the municipality using the main forces, and to take over municipal buildings with part of the forces in order to protect the population and material wealth, and to secure the functioning of the Serbian government and peaceful life in Sanski Most. Readiness for operations at 2200 hours on 19 April 1992." If you go directly above paragraph 4, Mr. Krajisnik, you'll see a reference which directs the 6th Krajina Brigade shall occupy, and it gives a number of axes and directions which the 6th Krajina Brigade should operate. The evidence before this Chamber is that the 6th Krajina Brigade was Colonel Basara's unit. Now, Colonel Basara, being a JNA officer, participated, according to this directive and according to the evidence that's before this Trial Chamber, Mr. Krajisnik, in the attack and takeover of the parts of the municipality of Sanski Most. Mr. Krajisnik, prior to either May 1st, 1992, when you went to Lisbon, or prior to the 16th Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1992, were you aware that the Bosnian Serbs, with the assistance of the JNA, had taken over power in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I believe I didn't know. But I'm sure I don't know about this particular action, how they did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you learn, Mr. Krajisnik, for the first time, that the Bosnian Serbs had taken over power in the Muslim-majority municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Was it before the 16th or on the 16th? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to another document, Mr. Krajisnik. If we could turn to the document that is found at tab 105. 105 has an exhibit number, Your Honours; P1059. Mr. Krajisnik, this is a document from the command of the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, it's dated the 19th of December, 1994, and it is addressed to the Drina Corps command. It is in part a retrospective document. Let me read to you the first portion of the first paragraph: "On 20 April, 1992, the forces of the Yugoslav army and the formed unit coordinated by the SDS Crisis Staff liberated the town of Vlasenica." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the same question to you: Prior to the 1st of May, 1992, before you went back to Lisbon, and also prior to the 16th -- to the 12th of May, 1992, the 16th Assembly session, were you aware that the JNA, in conjunction with Bosnian Serb forces, had liberated the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very clear, as far as all of your questions are concerned, possibly I did know that these areas were liberated. I never knew what forces were used to do that. And this being in concert between the JNA local units, I didn't know that. So if there are some documents, I would be happy to comment on them. The JNA was there. I'm not excluding that, that it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It consisted of people from that area as well. Perhaps there were some people from Serbia too, but I don't know. I don't know when I heard of Vlasenica. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to another document, Mr. Krajisnik. It's found at tab 113.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1210, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document, Mr. Krajisnik, is a short document, two pages. It is from the 17th Corps command, the JNA unit, dated the 26th of April, 1992. It's very urgent. It's a decision to conduct combat operations and it is directed to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and to the 2nd Military District command. And if you turn to paragraph 1 of the document, you can see that the author of this document, the author was Major General Milan Nedeljkovic says, and I quote: "I have made the following decisions: Upon completion of preparations, regrouping and necessary reassignment, units located in Bosnian Posavina (Operation Group 1, Tactical Group 17 and 395th Motorised Brigade), in cooperation with the Serbian Territorial Defence and police units, and with aerial and artillery support, are to start with offensive, defensive and other various combat activities." It goes on to say, in this document, Mr. Krajisnik, at paragraph 2.1, under the paragraph that deals with the unit tasks, it says: "Make adequate preparations, regroup and concentrate forces, then with aerial and artillery support and in cooperation with Lijesce TO units, launch an attack along the chosen axis, break up the enemy, inflict as heavy losses as possible, and reach the Sava River south-west of Bosanski Brod as soon as possible, cleanse Bosanski Brod, capture it and destroy the bridge on the Sava River in Bosanski Brod." If you go down to paragraph 2.2, Mr. Krajisnik, it says: "Perform the necessary regrouping with the artillery and -- with the aerial and artillery support and in cooperation with the Serbian TO and police unit prevent the OS RH from crossing the Sava River in the zone of responsibility, at the same time breaking up attacks of paramilitary formations and infiltrated sabotage terrorist groups." And finally, paragraph 2.3, for the 395th Motorised Brigade, it says: "In cooperation with TO and police units and with aerial and artillery support, the brigade is to prevent the OS RH from crossing the Sava River in the brigade's zone, exercise combat control of the territory, prevent interethnic conflicts, and constantly control roads in its zone of responsibility." Now, this document, Mr. Krajisnik, again shows that in April of 1992, in the area of the Posavina, the JNA was working along with territorial police units, Serbian Territorial Defence units and police units in offensive and defensive operations. Were you unaware of that, of these operations taking place, Mr. Krajisnik, unaware of the JNA assisting the Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence and police units in these kinds of operations in an area that later was to be defined as a strategic objective of the Bosnian Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that none of this was done by the JNA. Not a single one of these things that is contained in the order. They didn't take Brod, they didn't get to Sava, they didn't take the road - nothing. I'm aware of that. And I know that at that time, Mr. Efendic issued an order to block all barracks. He probably asked for the protection of the JNA, did he? I mean, Mr. Efendic, the commander of the Muslim forces. He issued this order to have JNA barracks sealed off. As for all of this contained in this order, none of it was done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krajisnik, let's turn our attention to Bratunac municipality, which again was a Muslim-majority municipality. The evidence before this Court, Mr. Krajisnik, was that power was taken over in the municipality on the 17th of April, and ethnic cleansing in the municipality commenced on the 9th of May, 1992. The evidence also before this Court, Mr. Krajisnik, is that there -- the participants in the ethnic cleansing on the 9th of May, 1992, and in the disarming of Muslim settlements before the ethnic cleansing began on that date, included a small armoured JNA unit under the command of an individual named Captain Reljic. The evidence also before this Court, Mr. Krajisnik, is that the JNA participated in the planning and the execution of the ethnic cleansing of the village of Glogova. Now, again, Mr. Krajisnik, when did you first learn, prior to the 16th session of the Assembly, about the takeover of power in the village of -- in the municipality of Bratunac? When did you learn that for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Was it before or then? I really don't know. As for how it was taken, that's what I heard from this man here, Mr. -- oh, Deronjic, yes, but I did not know that Bratunac was in Serb hands, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you learn for the first time, Mr. Krajisnik, that the village of Glogova and other Muslim settlements in the Bratunac municipality had been ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I never learned of that. I did not hear that it was cleansed. I heard that it was liberated. I had no idea what Glogova was and who was there. I mean, perhaps there is some information, but really over here I heard from Deronjic what happened in Glogova. I only heard about crimes committed against Serbs throughout the war. That's the only thing that I heard. And there is tonnes of evidence to point to that; books, brochures, what have you not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let me focus your attention on the events in Bratunac. When did you hear for the first time that Bratunac had been liberated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear about it prior to the 16th Assembly session on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. Well, maybe I did, maybe I didn't. I don't know. But I heard that I learned about -- but I know that I heard about it in 1992. But it would be dishonest if I were to say before or later because I cannot say exactly when it was that I heard about it and who it was that I heard about it. Let me just tell you something else. Immediately after Mr. Deronjic came, the government sent their own people to the ground. That's in government records. I didn't know about it at the time. Maybe they knew; I don't know. You have that in the government records. I found it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, shortly after the events in Glogova and shortly after Bratunac was liberated, 400 Bosnian Muslim civilians appeared in Pale. Does that in any way refresh your recollection and give you the -- an ability to think back on when you first learned of the events in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the people who were in Pale, I knew about them. And this is the information, that people from the leadership of Pale were very upset and Mr. Deronjic, in revolt, sent the Muslims to the leadership in Pale. That's the only thing I know. And then people carried this through, and I had no idea who they were, what this was all about, what happened. Even then I didn't know what Glogova was. I mean to this day -- well, okay, to this day, I have found out. It's some village. In 1991, I know that there was unrest in Bratunac. I mentioned that. Between the Serbs and Muslims, when those two people were killed, when I was president of the Assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, based on the evidence that you've heard in this Court, and based on the evidence that I presented you with today, it's -- do you dispute the fact, Mr. Krajisnik, that the JNA was involved in the attacks and the takeover of power in various municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina prior to the 1st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with the best of intentions, on the basis of what I'm reading now, if the JNA was there, and it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it certainly participated in the fighting. Now, was this fighting by way of an offensive or defence, I cannot say, but as the only regular armed force, it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was not on the Muslim side, it was not on the Croat side because they had turned into its enemies. That's clear. And I cannot say anything that's different from that. Now, I cannot say whether it was attacking or whether it was defending itself because Efendic said surround all the barracks, don't give them water, don't give them electricity. That I know. It would be dishonest of me to say now that they were sitting there and watching television or whatever. That's not correct.
