For the sake of the truth, I have to say that the JNA for the most part took care of itself because they had experienced a catastrophe in Croatia and Slovenia and they were afraid that they would be under siege, and they were under siege in Sarajevo, and they did whatever they could to protect their own members who were from Serbia, and they were there at the time, whereas the local population remained there, of course. Of course, I'm not denying -- I'm not denying that they took part in the fighting but I do not know in which way. I cannot confirm this, I cannot deny this, whether it launched any offensives; maybe it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in fact the JNA was coordinating with the Bosnian Serb leadership, on both the republic and the municipal level, prior to the 12th of May of, 1992, and you were aware of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two questions there really [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, let's start with I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the JNA was coordinating with the municipal leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, and that information was being conveyed to the republican level. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all let me answer your question as far as the municipalities are concerned. Wherever the JNA happened to be, it had to cooperate with the civilian authorities. And it did cooperate with the authorities, the Serb authorities, because it was not in the Muslim territories. And that's why they had to leave all their weapons behind and to get out, if they survived. If they were in Serb territories, they cooperated with the Serb authorities. If they were in the Muslim territories, they were blocked, that's true, so they could not cooperate with the authorities. Now, I'm so sorry, but what was your other question? The republican authorities? The republican level?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I asked you if you were aware that the Bosnian JNA was cooperating with the JNA on a municipal level, and I think you answered that question. I want to direct your attention to the item that is found in tab 111, Mr. Krajisnik, if you could take a look at that. That has a number already. It's Prosecution Exhibit 653. This, Mr. Krajisnik, is a letter, it bears the stamp of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it's dated the 23rd of March, 1992. It's for the attention of Minister Ostojic, and it is from the president of the Serbian Municipality of Kalesija, Petar Jankovic. And in this letter to Minister Ostojic, he indicates that the situation in Kalesija is complex and unpredictable, and in the penultimate paragraph he says, "Political and strategic decisions are being coordinated with the corps command in the 4th Armoured Brigade. I wish you success in the creation of Serbian state in BH." Now, Minister Ostojic is Velibor Ostojic; is that correct, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you met with Mr. Ostojic frequently in the period of time prior to the 12th of May, 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic worked in the party and he was in the government. I was in the Assembly. So it wasn't often but I did meet with him. Not often for sure. Well, I mean, it wasn't very few times either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he -- did Mr. Ostojic keep you informed about the developments that were occurring in the municipalities and particularly the events where -- for example, in Kalesija where the situation was both complex and unpredictable?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no municipality of Kalesija. Secondly, this man Petar Jankovic is an unusual man. I don't want to phrase it differently. Mr. Deronjic mentioned him, if you remember, that he was the best man of Commander Jankovic from Tuzla. How should I put this? What he's saying here is a pure pamphlet. Mr. Ostojic probably just put this away as soon as he received this document. It has nothing to do with a system of support or anything. This man was no president because Kalesija was not a municipality. Well, they established something on their own but it was never officially proclaimed. You will see that Momcilo Micic said that to you. That Tesic at one meeting of the Assembly said we formed Kalesija, nobody knew that we had formed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, are you disputing what Mr. Jankovic says, that the political and strategic decisions were being coordinated with the corps command and the 4th Armoured Brigade? Are you taking issue with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If his friend, his close friend, his best man, was corps commander, as Deronjic said, I believe that he did this along private -- through private channels. If he was not his best friend, then this corps commander is a fool for having talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to another document, Mr. Krajisnik. It's tab 112, and tab 112, Exhibit P529, tab 263, this is a document that's a very brief document, Mr. Krajisnik. It is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 112, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This has been exhibited before. This is a document that is from the 2nd -- from the JNA 2nd Military District reserve command post. It's dated the 6th of April and it's directed to the command of the 2nd Military District operations centre, and it is a regular operations report, Mr. Krajisnik. It is from Colonel Branko Filipovic, and in the penultimate paragraph, Colonel Filipovic says, "We have maintained constant contact and coordination of operations with the Pale Crisis Staff." So this document, Mr. Krajisnik, is another individual - this time a JNA officer - referring to coordinating with the Bosnian Serb authorities, this time in the municipality of Pale. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, were you aware that -- of the coordination between the JNA and the Pale Crisis Staff authorities prior to May the 1st of 1992 or prior to the 16th Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about this contact. Before that, I had been in Pale only once. So that's it as far as this contact is concerned. Later, when I came in April, it was already different. As far as what I can see here -- sorry, it's the 6th of April. The 6th of April, 1992. I wasn't there. I just had this graduation party before that, that I celebrated in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let us turn, then, Mr. Krajisnik, to another document. This is a document, Mr. Krajisnik, that is found at tab 114. This needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one, where the translation was inserted? Is that right? Yes. Yes. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's tab 114, Mr. Krajisnik. I'll identify the document for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, if I could get a number and then I'll identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1211, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is a document that is from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the Ministry of Defence, it is dated the 27th of April. It is to the 2nd Military District command. It's a request for reinforcement of active duty military personnel, and the author of this document is the minister, Colonel Bogdan Subotic. I'll read the first paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik: "In view of the essential need to bring the Territorial Defence in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to the basic level of manpower, in accordance with an agreement reached and a promise made in Belgrade, we request your urgent assistance in providing us with the following officers:" And then cast your eye on this document, Mr. Krajisnik. You will see that item number 1, the Republican Territorial Defence Staff, they identified the positions that are needed. Item number 2, the Sarajevo Territorial Defence city staff, they identify the positions that are needed, and they identify persons as well. And for the Doboj region in item number 3, they do the same. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, let me ask you, Minister Subotic -- first of all, were you aware of this order, Mr. Krajisnik, prior to the 1st of May, 1992, before you went to Lisbon? That the minister of defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was asking the 2nd Military District command to supply the Ministry of Defence with personnel? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was a commander of Territorial Defence, but I don't know how he was appointed. He was there briefly and then he left. He had seen Lukic [as interpreted]. And I don't know about this communication. It was within the province of the minister, so he dealt with it on his own. It's nothing unusual. All of these people that he requested, they were all from Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you meet with Colonel Subotic, the minister of defence, at any time prior to the 1st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I frequently -- in fact not frequently, but I met with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he not tell you that he had been making -- that he had made a request for army personnel, active duty military personnel, to bring up the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina forces up to proper manpower levels? He didn't bring that up with you at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out the possibility that he said that but it was within his jurisdiction any way. We did not have Territorial Defence. And all these things that he did were rightly within his province because the Territorial Defence wasn't functioning properly. He was requesting staff, just like Muslims had their own TO, we should have our own TO, because the Serb TO had been proclaimed but did not operate. You see, it didn't operate until April, since all this stuff was missing at the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the document from Minister Subotic in the first paragraph refers to an agreement that was reached and a promise that was made in Belgrade. Can you enlighten us as to what that agreement and promise, what they were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically whether it's related to this but I know that whenever there was any discussion about -- I don't believe there was any discussion about it at that time, but when the decision about the withdrawal of the JNA was taken, it was said that all staff from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the JNA could remain in our army, but I don't think that relates to this TO issue. Because it was later agreed that staff should come over. I don't know about this agreement. The one I mentioned took place later. I know about the other agreement, when our army was being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let's turn to another document, then, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the document that's found on -- at tab 102. Again, Mr. Krajisnik, the focus of these questions is the neutrality of the JNA. And if we turn to document that is found at tab 102, it bears a Prosecution Exhibit number P892, Ewan Brown tab 74. This, Mr. Krajisnik, is a document that's dated the -- first of all, it's from the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Autonomous Region of Krajina war staff in Banja Luka. It's dated the 6th of May, 1992, and it is the telephone numbers of members of the Krajina Autonomous Region war staff. Number 8, General Momir Talic, is a JNA general. And if you cast your eye, Mr. Krajisnik, on a number of people whose names are quite familiar in this Court: Radoslav Brdjanin, he was a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if you go to number 3, Vojo Kupresanin, he was a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you know Predrag Radic, number 5, the man identified at number 5?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have contact with him prior to the 1st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he testified that I had not been in contact with him. I didn't. Even later I had very few and rare contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the Stojan Zupljanin, who was identified in number 10, did you have contacts with him prior to the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I had very few contacts with Zupljanin throughout the war; few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you look at the names I did not identify, did you have contact with any of those other persons in that list prior to the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether I had been in contact with anybody, but I really don't remember being in contact with anyone concerning this document. Not one single person. As far as this document is concerned, I didn't even know that there was a war staff. I certainly wasn't in contact with General Talic, because I had seen the man only once before the war, and even that was by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in your contacts with your fellow legislators, Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Kupresanin, did they inform you at any time prior to the 12th of May, 1991, that the JNA was actively participating with them in -- and assisting them in their regions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 27th of March until this date, I had no contact whatsoever with MPs and they did not report to me what was going on, whether the JNA had been in contact with them or not. But I told you already: I personally believed that if JNA existed there, it did take part. I just don't know in which form; in offensive operations, defensive operations, but it was there at that time. There is no dispute about that. We did not have a Territorial Defence, so the JNA probably took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We all can agree, Mr. Krajisnik, that the JNA was present in Bosnia prior to the 12th of May. I've shown you a number of documents, you've heard considerable amount of testimony regarding the participation of the JNA in cooperation and in coordination with Serbian -- Bosnian Serb forces, taking over municipalities and taking over power in municipalities. Mr. Krajisnik, do you still assert that the JNA was entirely neutral in the events prior to the 12th of May, 1992? Or does the evidence that you've seen in this courtroom change your view and opinion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Your Honours, I will repeat what I have already said: The Yugoslav People's Army played a neutral role all the way until the moment when Croats and Muslims started viewing it as a hostile army and turned against it. The moment when they started laying siege to the barracks, which is at this time, when they started cutting off their electricity and water supply, they had only one natural ally in that area; the Serb authorities. In Muslim areas, there were no bases of the JNA because they had left their weapons, up and went. As for cooperation and what forms it took, I can only tell you what I have seen myself in Sarajevo. Cooperation with Mr. Kukanjac and his public appearances. I'm speaking about that level. As for the local level, I gave you the example of Rajlovac, where the local commander distributed weapons among Serbs and Muslims equally. And my modest [as interpreted] about the local cooperation, cooperation at the local level, is modest. That is my entire knowledge about the role of the Yugoslav People's Army, and I hope I have answered your question, Mr. Prosecutor. The JNA lived a disaster in Bosnia because it barely managed to pull out, with enormous losses. It was victimised in Sarajevo, in Tuzla, and they barely pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question? Mr. Krajisnik, you said several times, "We had no TO." On from -- for what period would that be valid? Did finally a Serb TO come into existence and on from what date, if so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 6th of April or maybe the 7th of April, I'm not sure, right at the beginning of April, the TO of the Serb Republic was proclaimed, but in practice, as I said, it did not function, and we can see that from one of those papers where it says on the 26th of April, they still have no commander. In practice there were just armed people, armed citizens. That's why I said we didn't have a TO in practical terms. It only existed on paper. I don't know how it was in municipalities. Maybe it did function in some places, because it was a structure that existed before the war, in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. The structure was there. But what I'm saying is that we had this commander, Vidoje Lukic, and Subotic and when we asked them, Are you capable of doing something? and they said no. From that, I conclude that they did not function. They were impotent; they couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say that you don't know how it was in the municipalities. Maybe it did function in some places. Most of the questions put to you by Mr. Harmon were about what happened in the municipalities, and when you said "We did not have a Territorial Defence," I understood that to be your answer as well in relation to the municipalities, but I might have misunderstood you. You said, "From the 27th of March until this date, I had no contact whatsoever with MPs and they did not report to me what was going on, whether the JNA had been in contact with them or not." I understood that to be reporting or a lack of reporting on what happened in the municipalities. And in that same answer, you said, "We did not have a Territorial Defence so the JNA probably took part." I'm a bit confused about what your testimony now is, whether there was no TO at all or whether you did not know about the functioning of the TO in some of the municipalities, because all the questions were about cooperation on the municipality level primarily. I'm not saying that nothing related to the central level but that was at least an important part of the questions put to you and the answers you gave. Could you please enlighten me in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I said we did not have a Territorial Defence, I went on to explain that this commander, and the minister, and the first thing you need to have an efficient Territorial Defence, you have to have those two people in place, and I said they were impotent. Something cannot function well in municipalities if you do not have the vertical line starting with the commander and all the following elements of organisation. That's why I gave that negative assessment of the Territorial Defence, which had been established on paper. When I said Did it function in municipalities? I said the TO existed in pre-war Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was supposed to be a municipal commander at the municipal level and maybe that person had organised a TO. I didn't know about that, but I don't rule out the possibility. So much about Territorial Defence. The Prosecutor, however, asked me whether I had contacted with MPs, Brdjanin, Kupresanin, and others, and whether they had informed me about cooperation with the JNA. I said I had no contact with them because there had been no sessions from the 27th of March until the 12th of May, and they did not report to me about it. And I didn't know about that war staff. That was my attempt to briefly explain in response to two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon. But if you have a subject, or if you want to finish this subject in a couple of minutes, fine. Otherwise, we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's take a break, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Harmon, I have a few procedural decisions -- well, as a matter of fact, it's a few procedural matters to raise. It's about exhibits. First of all, in regard to the Prosecution's evidence of destruction in 1992, a CD was given to the Defence on the 25th of May to review, and two sets of photographs were made available to the Defence on the 29th of May. In an e-mail to a legal officer on the 26th of May, the Defence has requested seven days to review this material. Today, the Defence informed the Chamber that it is in the process of discussing this material with Mr. Krajisnik. The Chamber grants the Defence until Monday, the 12th of June, to raise any objections to the material. These objections, as well as all other objections referred to in this decision, may be raised orally at a suitable moment in court or submitted in a brief written filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour. I can inform the Court there will be objections. I'm going to talk to Mr. Harmon first of all and then choose my moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The date was set because earlier, as a matter of fact, there was some time asked for in e-mail but the Chamber never decided on how much time would be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, I really am very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I continue: The parties have submitted the following documents in relation to double pension legislation: That's D236, the law on the rights of fighters, disabled servicemen, and family of those killed in the Republika Srpska homeland defence war, printed in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska, dated 21st of May 2001. Then D237, a letter from Slavko Basic, director of the pension and disability insurance fund of Republika Srpska, dated the 3rd of April, 2006. P1178, Articles 94 and 157 of the law on pension and disability insurance. And P1179, Article 42 of the law on pension and disability insurance. These exhibits are hereby admitted into evidence. On the 25th of May, the Prosecution submitted the decision on the return of displaced persons to the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, published in issue number 8/92 of the Official Gazette of the Serbian people. This item, however, is already admitted into evidence as Exhibit number P529, tab 165. On that same day, the Prosecution also submitted the correction of the decision on the return of expelled persons to the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, published in issue number 11/92 of the Official Gazette of the Serbian people. This item is not yet in evidence and needs to be assigned an exhibit number. Madam Registrar, could we please have a number for that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1212, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Defence has until Monday, the 12th of June, to raise any objection to this item or it will be admitted into evidence without further action. All documents and translations have been received by the registrar regarding the following items: D144, an extract from newspaper Dnevni Avaz, dated the 19th of May, 2005; D170, a letter to Ambassador Cutileiro from Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic; D177, a video clip of the television programme Club 91; D178 an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic dated the 16th of July, 1991; D179, an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic dated the 11th of December, 1991; D183, an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic dated the 4th of October, 1991; D186, an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic dated 3rd of December, 1991; D190 through and including D192F, D195 and D196, which are maps on which Mr. Krajisnik has marked various items; P1086, minutes of the first meeting of the committee for mass communications dated the 8th of October, 1991; D1149, a postal money order dated the 30th of December, 1991. The parties have until Monday the 12th of June to raise any objections or on that date these items will be admitted into evidence without further action. With regard to all other exhibits, the Chamber is hereby setting a deadline of Tuesday the 20th of June for the parties to provide the registrar with any outstanding missing items and translations. The parties should refer to the exhibit lists which are continuously updated and provided by the registrar. Thereafter, the parties will have until the 27th of June to raise any objections or the items tendered by the 20th of June deadline will be admitted into evidence without further action. This is, of course, without prejudice to the possibility that the Chamber itself may decide not to admit any piece of evidence for other reasons. The registrar has received English translations for a group of documents which were provisionally marked on the 24th of May, 2006, as Exhibits D197 through and including D216. As we did with documents which were received from Mr. Krajisnik at a later stage, the Chamber would like to leave it to the parties to review the material and to indicate to the Chamber which, if any, of these documents they wish to offer into evidence. Lastly, Exhibit D169 is hereby admitted under seal. It is in fact the pseudonym sheet of Witness D24 which was not formally admitted into evidence. This concludes the Chamber's order, and Mr. Harmon, I'd like to invite you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, will you agree with me that in late 1991 and early 1992, prior to the commencement of the war in Bosnia, the fact that the JNA was providing voluminous amounts of arms and materiel to only one of the parties, potential parties to the conflict, the Bosnian Serbs, that that was not a neutral act?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You believe that the JNA, in providing volumes of arms, materiel, to only the Bosnian Serbs, was an act that showed neutrality; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether at that time the JNA was providing only the Serbs with weapons or whether it was providing weapons at all. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before the war start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at your evidence, because you gave evidence on a number of days, Mr. Krajisnik, in respect of the JNA providing arms. On day 259, your testimony was that you did not know in which way the Serbs were arming themselves or if they were arming themselves. On day 262, in response to a question put to you by Judge Hanoteau you answered: "But I emphasised I did not have any information at the time that the Serb side was arming itself." On day 268, you were asked a question whether the Bosnian Serbs had armed themselves and you said, "As for things I heard second-hand, stories circulated that people were receiving weapons, and I heard some stories like that, like rumours but nothing specific." And finally, you were asked a question by Judge Hanoteau in respect of the knowledge of Dr. Karadzic and his knowledge of arming, and your answer, in part, was that arming people was a secret. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you travelled often to Belgrade and representatives, including Dr. Karadzic and other representatives of the Bosnian Serb administration, travelled to Belgrade, and they held discussions with both political and military leaders prior to the commencement of the war. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've said that before the war I did not go to Belgrade often, because I was an official. I could not go like someone who was just a party member. I didn't go often but I was there a few times. I don't know exactly how many times. For the most part when we would go to some conference or something like that, people had to know about each and every time I went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to you, Dr. Karadzic went to Belgrade numerous occasions, didn't he, Mr. Krajisnik, prior to the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Well, not that much but I don't know exactly to what extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in Bosnia, Mr. Krajisnik, you had meetings with representatives of the JNA prior to the beginning of the war, as did Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated here that I was in a delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the top echelons of the military in Sarajevo. We also had a meeting in Belgrade. But I didn't have any other meetings with the JNA except for what I said, that I had a meeting with Kukanjac once the war had already started. That's what I remember. Perhaps there was some meeting that I really cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was fully informed and aware of the fact that the JNA was providing weapons to the Bosnian Serbs prior to the beginning of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that on the basis of all these papers that I saw, Mr. Karadzic was only engaged in political activity aimed at helping the mobilisation of people who would be under the JNA. I don't see any logic involved in this. Why would he give Serbs weapons if they were under the JNA? I'm speaking only on the basis of logic. I don't have any other knowledge apart from that. Whether there was anything else apart from that, I cannot say by way of testimony because it would be a sin for me to say something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's take a look at tab 115, Mr. Krajisnik. This is an exhibit that's P46. This is an intercept between Dr. Karadzic and Mihalj Kertes on the 24th of June, 1991. And you will recall, Mr. Krajisnik, that Mr. Kertes was identified in the testimony of Miroslav Deronjic as the person to whom he and Mr. Zekic went in 1991 to visit in Belgrade and who was principally involved in the providing of arms to Eastern Bosnia. Now, in this intercept, Mr. Krajisnik, it has been played before in this court, you'll see on the first page Mr. Kertes, the fifth box down with Mr. Kertes, and on page 1 of the English, Your Honour, again the fifth box down, Mr. Kertes informs Dr. Karadzic, "This could be going much better. However the main problem is that Junackovic is holding up everything." First of all, do you know who Mr. Junackovic is? Is that a name that's familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. The next time, two boxes -- the next box down with Mr. Kertes, he says -- I'm reading from the second sentence: "He wouldn't let anything -- it's probably be done. Jovica's hands are tied. Jovica went mad and I'm worried that he'll soon be your patient." Now in this intercept, the evidence was adduced about it, Jovica was Jovica -- was identified as Jovica Stanisic, and who was a state Serb minister of state security, and Slobo, who we'll see later, was identified as Mr. Milosevic. If you read down to Mr. Karadzic -- I mean Mr. Kertes, down -- the fourth box down following the passage that I quoted, Mr. Kertes says, "For 50 pieces of furniture, he held until 5 p.m." Now, on page 3 of the English, at the top of the English, and I'm sorry, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to give you some time to try to find this passage. I didn't locate it. Mr. Kertes -- actually, it's the second box after the passage that I just read -- says, "If we are going to do 50 a day, then --" if you go down four more boxes where Mr. Kertes again speaks, and this is on page 3 of the English, Mr. Kertes says, "No, Slobo has given Jovica and me carte blanche, but then he's Jovica's boss and he's driving Jovica crazy." And Karadzic says, "I see." And Kertes says, "He wouldn't let him do anything. Jovica ..." Karadzic: "Yes." Kertes: "He's gone crazy. He rang me twice today and he couldn't ... believe they did 50 pieces today. He let them -- he let him five hours there." Karadzic: "Right. Okay, tell me ... other, other things. Is there any other news?" Kertes: "Well, we're prepared to do everything ..." And this intercept is, the testimony of Mr. Deronjic was that was coded language between Mr. Kertes and Dr. Karadzic dealing with the provision of arms. Now, you can see, Mr. Krajisnik, that the date of this is the 24th of June, 1991. My question to you, Mr. Krajisnik, is: Between the 24th of June, 1991, and the 12th of May, 1992, did Dr. Karadzic at any time inform you that the Bosnian Serbs were receiving arms from Belgrade? Or did he leave you completely in the dark on that significant event and development?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am going to object, Your Honour, because surely my learned friend needs to have groundwork first of all and ask Mr. Krajisnik if he accepts the proposition that Mr. Deronjic advanced in relation to this particular intercept. That's the first stage. And the second stage of the question he has just asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- let me ask you this question,

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When Mr. Kertes is dealing with 50 pieces of furniture, you knew who Mr. Kertes was, didn't you, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who Kertes is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he a furniture merchant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no idea what the furniture is. Maybe it's what you're saying, maybe it's something different. I don't know. Well, obviously, it is some kind of code, so kind of coded language. But it doesn't have to mean it's weapons. Maybe it's something else. Maybe it's something much bigger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I take it that you're unable to assist us in that code language, so let me go to the second part of my question, Mr. Krajisnik. Did Dr. Karadzic at any time between the 24th of June, 1991, and the 12th of May, 1992, ever tell you that Belgrade was providing weapons to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've said that I heard rumours. I can tell you what I knew about weapons, if you're interested, and I can also answer your question, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, please. Answer my question, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember having talked to Mr. Karadzic about any kind of arming, and I'll tell you what it was that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, Mr. Krajisnik, beside Dr. Karadzic, did you hear from any other person who was in either the Bosnian Serb administration, either the minister of defence, any of your other colleagues, that the Bosnian Serbs were receiving weapons from Belgrade? Or was that something that you assert today in this Court you were completely ignorant of, no one ever informed you of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were three affairs. Serbs were blamed for two of them and Muslims for one. It had to do with trucks full of weapons that were captured, and a prosecutor even let the suspects go, and so on and so forth. So I heard lots of rumours, locally. There was a debate at an Assembly meeting about this problem. So it is not that it was totally unknown that there was some kind of arming but I didn't want to get involved in that kind of thing. There are law enforcement agencies and let them deal with that. As for Mr. Karadzic, I did not talk to him about such problems. I did not know that the Serbs were being armed. As for this conversation with Kertes, I don't know. If this had to do with arming, that is. And, please, just one more thing, I'm sorry. When Mr. Deronjic testified, Mr. Rajko Dukic spoke for the newspapers. We have that. And he said that Mr. Deronjic's statement has nothing to do with anything. He spoke up on the very next day, and we have that piece of paper, and if you want, I can provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, isn't it a fact, Mr. Krajisnik, that Dr. Karadzic did raise with you directly the fact that the Serbs did not have enough arms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. When he said the Serbs do not have enough weapons, I said, well, let's move on. And I did move on. But he did not tell me whether they got weapons, how they got weapons. The Serbs could have armed themselves. Later on I saw that Serbs had weapons, all Serbs, or rather, everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina had weapons. So if you want to look at the intercept and you will see what my answers were. If I knew what this was all about, I would have said, What? And so and so forth. He says to me, Serbs do not have weapons, and the Muslims are establishing the police as their army. If I remember correctly, that's what he said in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, you anticipated my next question, Mr. Krajisnik, because we'll turn to tab 116. It's Prosecution Exhibit 67, tab 15. Also bears the number P154 and P292 KID 30511. Since you appear to be quite familiar with this intercept, Mr. Krajisnik, I won't direct you to the passages but I'll direct the Trial Chamber to the passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, this is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik on the 23rd of September, 1991, and it is a conversation, as Your Honours can see, at the first page, middle of the page, where Dr. Karadzic is -- says: "Well, our people are incapable of doing anything. Alija is trying to mobilise ... to create an army through expansion ... the unlimited expansion of part of the reserve force." Mr. Krajisnik says, "Protection, right?" Karadzic says: "Mobilising the reserve force. We would have to call him urgently, urgently ... the two of us, to sit down with him and tell him that that's civil war." On page 2 in the English, Your Honour, starting at the third box from the top, Dr. Karadzic says, "Yes. Well, all right, what, what ... I mean in Serb areas they don't have enough weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Hm?" Karadzic: "They don't have enough weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "All right, but we're analysing, Radovan, please. Let me tell you something, I would like to ask you for something in connection to that. We should weigh things well. What you said last night was smart. We must always see what that means."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic raised a very, very serious issue with you on this telephone call, the Serbs didn't have enough weapons, and we have heard evidence, including your evidence, that the Serbs were concerned about genocide being committed against the Serb people. And what Dr. Karadzic is saying to you in this intercept is the Serbs don't have enough weapons. As a result of that conversation that you had with Dr. Karadzic, that conversation on the 23rd of September, 1991, did you have a conversation with Dr. Karadzic to explore the potential dangers to the Serb people that Dr. Karadzic, at least, had foreseen and foreshadowed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the interpretation is not good. Mr. Prosecutor, the subject here, the central subject here, is that Mr. Karadzic is upset over the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic is establishing his own army and he is aggravating the situation. And I'm trying to calm him down and he said we haven't got weapons, and I simply moved on to another subject. In three or four days we were supposed to have an Assembly meeting and we were not supposed to impose solutions to one another. And you know that on the 30th of September we had an Assembly meeting. It has nothing to do with weapons here. And I was not naive. There was shooting all over the place in Croatia. So there were weapons all over Bosnia, but I was not discussing this that somebody was coming from Belgrade, from Podgorica and I don't know where else. The central point here is that Mr. Izetbegovic is trying to establish his own army through the reserve police, and I said, okay, calmly, let's take it easy. That's the point. Bosnia was full of weapons because volunteers came from Croatia, wherever. I did not know who had weapons and how much and who was distributing weapons to who, and that's what I said. And that became so obvious in Bosnia. As soon as the shooting started, everybody had weapons in Bosnia. I would be naive if I were to say that I didn't know. We saw people who were marching with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as always, we would see it only on the other side, not in our own ranks, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, my question to you was, as a result of that conversation that you had with Dr. Karadzic, did you have a conversation with Dr. Karadzic to explore the potential dangers to the Serb people that Dr. Karadzic, at least, had foreseen and foreshadowed, that is the lack of arms by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have answered. What was discussed here were reserve forces. Whether there were other conversations has nothing to do with this conversation. I could have said something about what you were saying now but not in connection with this conversation. This conversation had to do with the reserve police, and that's what I was talking about. And perhaps I was having a discussion with him about something completely different that was totally unrelated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said I could have had -- I could have said something about that -- about what you were saying but not in connection with this conversation. Okay. Did you have a conversation with Dr. Karadzic in connection perhaps not with this conversation but with any other conversation about the Serbs not having enough weapons and needing to acquire weapons?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. If you were to ask me now, I don't know. Give me this conversation, then I'll tell you what I discussed. As for everything I've said so far, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, in November of 1991, you were aware, weren't you, that the Serbs indeed were better armed than the other parties, potential parties, to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In November, 1991, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. Show me that and I'll explain it to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's turn to tab 125. This is an exhibit, it's the plebiscite speech, it's Prosecution Exhibit 1191, and let's turn to two portions of this speech, Mr. -- For the Trial Chamber's benefit and counsel's benefit I'm going to direct Your Honours and counsel to page 5 of the English, third paragraph from the bottom, and I'm going to direct Your Honour -- and Mr. Krajisnik for your benefit, that is found on the page that bears the ERN number 00270633.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: About mid-page. And in this particular speech, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic says, in the middle of that paragraph that begins with the words, "There is a chance that we will fight. In that case, let the chips fall where they may." In the English version, if you go down about four lines, Mr. Karadzic says, "They know we are better armed." Now, also --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just tell me where this is exactly? I don't know. I mean, you keep leaving certain sections out and I can't see it very well here. Yes, yes, now I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to direct Your Honour's attention to page 10, to the last paragraph that starts with, "So that's it." If you go, Mr. Krajisnik, to the second-to-last page in the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, the page that bears the ERN number with the last three digits 638, and direct your attention to the middle of the page. Second to the last page, Mr. Krajisnik. And in this part of Mr. Karadzic's speech, he says -- I'll read part of the paragraph: "The army is here. By chance, their aims and our aims coincide 100 per cent. Do not leave that equipment and that army on its own. Don't! That would be a disgrace. We would lose the state if we lost that army. It's been a year now, you've seen it at rallies, Serbs have been asking for weapons. They are asking for weapons. We did not have weapons. They got some themselves, and they got themselves a lot. Finally, the army -- finally, there is the army, which is three times stronger. They even removed the red star. They have weapons, equipment and other materiel." So in November of 1991, at this particular speech, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic is affirming that the Serbs were better armed than their potential adversaries and that they had acquired lots of weapons. Mr. Krajisnik, were those facts about which you were entirely unaware?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, these are no facts. This is a political speech. It doesn't have to be incorrect necessarily, but for me to listen to this today, I mean, I never would have remembered this. He is saying, well, who has more weapons, and they were trying to resolve things on their own. It is obviously addressed to the other side, to avert them from their intentions. He is saying here we have the army, the army is armed, and so on. I'm not trying to say that the Serbs were not arming themselves, but I don't know about that. So what Karadzic is saying here, I mean, even if I were to listen to it today, I would not take it as the truth. I would take it as propaganda. I don't think that the Serbs did not have weapons, but at rallies, he says Serbs were asking for weapons, and we don't have them. I don't know how else I could explain this. If you think I heard this, believe me, this is as if I were hearing it for the first time. And I'm not saying that I was not there. I probably heard it, but it didn't mean a thing to me. The war was about to start. People kept saying that Muslims, Serbs, Croats, were selling, say, a cow in order to buy a rifle. There was talk like that all over the place. And I remember one rally, Karadzic saying we have weapons. And the people say, give us weapons, and he says but our weapons are peace, the truth. You have that speech. You can read it. I'd really say this if I knew it. There is no reason for me not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 117, Mr. Krajisnik. This is an intercept, Exhibit number P259. It's a conversation between yourself and Rajko Dukic. Mr. Krajisnik, this is a conversation that's been in evidence, and you're familiar with the contents of this intercept, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read this, just as the previous conversation. It had been produced here before. That's why I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic is the man who Mr. Deronjic identified as the person who was -- who informed he and Mr. Zekic to arm their municipalities on April or May of 1991. I would like you -- Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to read part of this intercept to you, and I'm referring, Your Honour, to the second page of the intercept, starting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I appreciate this has been exhibited. Can my learned friend help us to the date the Prosecution alleged this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask Mr. Krajisnik that question because this is undated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, after looking at this interview, when do you believe this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, although I would like to answer. I saw it here when you produced it. But it must be from 1991, the end of 1991, when there was this problem with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this conversation, Mr. Dukic is quite upset, as you can see, and Mr. Dukic says, and I'm reading, Mr. Krajisnik, starting at the fourth box from the bottom of the second page, fourth box of Mr. Dukic. He says: "No, my man, they should be told, if you want to, to work like human beings. If you don't want to, let us go our separate ways so we know what belongs to whom in the republic. Why would I, I live in the bigger fear that when I was born, my man." You answer: "I agree." Dukic: "My head is all under pressure, my man." You answer: "Earlier, earlier a bit, so we can have coffee." Now if you would be so kind, Mr. Krajisnik, as to read slowly in your language the response of Mr. Dukic to that, I would appreciate it, because I think there is a -- may be a potential translation error here. Would you kindly read that box in your language, very slowly, starting with "Od ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From mujahedins," or F word, "I ordered a thousand automatic weapons, my man. I will officially purchase them through the company. Fucking motherfuckers -" I apologise for this - "I will set up barricades there in seven days." "I apologise for this" was -- were my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then, okay. So Your Honours I do believe there is a translation error and we will -- we have a new translation for that but I can distribute that if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in this particular intercept, Mr. Dukic has informed you that he ordered a thousand automatic rifles and he was going to get them officially for the company. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you don't seem at all surprised by your answer to that -- by that statement by Mr. Dukic. And you were directly informed that thousand automatic weapons were to be acquired by Mr. Dukic. Can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. First of all, Mr. Dukic is very frustrated here because he's unable to complete the job that had been agreed with the Muslims concerning appointments in the MUP, and I'm trying to calm him down, to tell him that we should sit down together and have a coffee with him to persuade him not to do anything in that state of frustration. And he is saying, I've never been more afraid in my life. And he's afraid because he sees what the Muslims are doing; they are setting up barricades, whereas he's not allowed to set up barricades. Now, this last sentence that I just read out, Mr. Dukic says, I'll tell them, I'll purchase automatic weapons publicly for the company. Even after the war, Mr. Dukic had, in the bauxite plant, a so-called internal guard, internal security, and they really did have weapons, automatic weapons in that company. He's not referring to distributing arms to people, he's just saying out of frustration that I'm going to do that and we are going to hand them out. The consequence of what he's suggesting is not that he's going to distribute weapons but that he is unable to carry through this -- these appointments, because they were not letting him do that although it had been agreed. He had a security detail in the mine, and even after the war there were some objections and criticism that maybe it wasn't legal. Not an enormous amount but maybe a thousand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was not a thousand. Interpreter's correction: It was not a thousand or anything like that. It was 200 to 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, when Mr. Krajisnik reflects what has been said, he says, "I will purchase automatic weapons publicly for the company", whereas the transcript reads that he -- he ordered, which means that it has happened already, whereas the other language suggests that it's still to be done. I've got no idea whether there could be any doubt as to what was said, so therefore the parties are invited, since Mr. Krajisnik -- it might not be a matter of translation but it might be a matter of hearing what has been said. Of course, the translation we could easily check that by putting on the ELMO the relevant line and ask the interpreters what it says. Could we perhaps have the B/C/S original on the ELMO, and could we invite the interpreters, looking at the text in the third box from the bottom of the second page -- let me just check whether we have it. Yes, could the interpreters tell us where the three lines spoken by Mr. Rajko Dukic, whether it indicates that he will or that he -- he will order or he will purchase or that he ordered or did purchase?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The second sentence reads, "I have -- I have ordered a thousand pieces of automatic weapons, man." The third sentence reads, "I will officially purchase them or obtain them into the company."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. Then, of course, there is still a possibility that by listening to this audio recording, some mistake has been made. Mr. Josse, if there is any reason to believe this is wrong, I take it you'll check that on the basis of the CD on which this appears. It's just raising the issue, not because I have any reason to believe that it's wrongly understood but I noticed that Mr. Krajisnik, who as a matter of fact only read the text at this moment, he did not hear it, gave a different interpretation of what was said, which now turns out, at least, not to be in accordance with the B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll try and scrutinise the audio file, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least if you consider this to be useful. Then another matter is that -- for the registrar, that the -- what is it P259, the translation should be replaced by the improved translation, the new one, and the old one to be removed. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you have a conversation with Mr. Dukic afterwards, after this conversation, to follow up on what Mr. -- what Mr. Dukic had said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I did, and I didn't understand this as a serious threat either. I understood this as a speech by a frustrated man. If I failed to explain something, I would like to explain it. I just don't understand where the misunderstanding lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have concluded for the day. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have one additional question: Mr. Krajisnik, do you happen to know -- let me just -- the security personnel of the bauxite company Mr. Dukic was in charge of, do you happen to know how many men, approximately, were in these security personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I know that he had some security personnel after the war, and that there was some sort of problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you also told us that -- and that was -- we read it from a correction of the interpreters, that you said it was not an enormous amount but -- it was not a thousand or anything like that, it was 200 to 300. What's the source of the knowledge that it was 200 to 300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because when I was a member of the Presidency, we had problems there, and I know that he had his own security service, security detail, politically. I don't know which year it was, '87 or something. I just named a number off the cuff. And I know the MUP intervened at that point. It was something that happened in '87 -- '97, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you were referring to the number, you were referring to the strength of the security personnel in the bauxite mine? Is that a correct understanding, as you learned about it in a later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, I found out, there were political rifts in Republika Srpska. The police went there and ran into this security detail of the mine. There was some sort of respectable group there. I don't know how many. But, please, it's very important, there is a very important word that he said. He said, "I'll purchase officially." He didn't say "legally [as interpreted]." He will officially purchase a certain number of automatic weapons. That's how I understand it now. Not then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you were talking about 200 or 200 to 300, were you talking about men employed in the security services of the bauxite mine or were you talking about a number of -- an amount of weapons? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just saying any number. Not a thousand, but it -- I was saying it off the cuff. It could have been 200, 300. I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is, is the number about men or is the number about weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Men with weapons. That's what it could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking what you were referring to. You said it was not a thousand, it was 200 or 300, and I do understand that you had no precise knowledge, but were you talking about armed men of that service and are you then referring to what you learned later on, well, let's say after 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found out later, and I assumed that that could have been the number of the security detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to tell you how I now understand, after these additional questions, what I understand your testimony to be: That since you learned, well, let's say, after 1995, about the number of armed men being in the security department of the bauxite company, that from that, you make an inference that when he said at an earlier stage that he had ordered weapons and where he used the number a thousand, that it could not be correct because your knowledge goes as far as 200 to 300 armed men in the company only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about a thousand automatic weapons, I said that the reason he could have had for ordering weapons was this security service, the security detail, but I don't believe that there were 1.000 men. There were less on that security detail; 200 or 300. I only later learned about it. How many people he employed in that service during the war, I don't know. And whether there were a thousand of them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for these answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one correction. Page 80, line 16, the transcript reads, "He didn't say 'legally,'" I am told Mr. Krajisnik said "illegally."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just check, one second. Yes. That's how I understood the answer. Otherwise, it doesn't make much of a logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik was nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Officially." He didn't say "illegally" but, on the contrary, "officially." Yes, that's how I understood the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that was quite important, that's why I made the observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction, Mr. Josse. Mr. Krajisnik, I instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given, and we will adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
